props.name: OER at pH 2-12 essentially requires buffer molecules

evidence.quote: For pH values ranging from about 2 to 12, the OER reaction essentially requires buffer molecules that facilitate proton transport. In the absence of an explicit buffer base, either only water molecules or hydroxide ions could serve as proton-transporting buffer bases; both cannot support signiﬁcant current densities.

props.limitations: first-order model; proton-transport limitations at the catalyst–electrolyte interface and within the catalyst film are excluded; for water or OH− as proton acceptors Equation (15) is no longer exact
props.note: Attempt-3 fix: the statement's closing qualifier 'in the near-neutral pH region' was removed (replaced by 'over this pH 2-12 range') to align with the source's conclusion, which is stated for pH about 2-12 (p. 9, Conclusions, item 1), not only near-neutral pH.
props.scope: OER in aqueous electrolytes, pH about 2–12, per the presented first-order model
props.statement: For pH values from about 2 to 12, the oxygen-evolution reaction essentially requires dissolved buffer molecules to transport protons; in the absence of an added buffer base, neither water molecules nor hydroxide ions can support significant current densities over this pH 2-12 range.

props.name: water-species diffusion coefficients vs buffer bases

evidence.quote: Then Equation (15) predicts sizeable current densities, inter alia because the diffusion coefﬁcient (D) is about 10 times higher for H3O+ and ﬁve times higher for OH−than for the commonly used buffer bases (e.g., HPO42−/H2PO4−)

props.statement: Diffusion coefficients of the water species are higher than those of commonly used buffer bases: about 10 times higher for H3O+ and about 5 times higher for OH− than for buffer bases such as the HPO4²−/H2PO4− pair, which is why sizeable current densities are predicted in strongly acidic and alkaline electrolytes without an added buffer base.

props.name: maximal current density set by unprotonated buffer concentration

evidence.quote: In the presence of a buffer base, the maximal current density is determined by the concentration of unprotonated buffer molecules and, thus, by the solution pH and the pKa value of the used buffer, in line with experimental ﬁndings [15].
Thus, Jmax scales with the fraction of unprotonated buffer molecules.

props.scope: buffered electrolytes at high overpotentials (J approaching Jmax of Equation (16))
props.statement: In the presence of a buffer base, the maximal current density at high overpotentials is determined by the concentration of unprotonated buffer molecules, and thus by the solution pH and the pKa of the buffer; Jmax scales with the fraction of unprotonated buffer molecules.

evidence.note: second-hand: model prediction of reference [28], reported by the source

props.name: Nernstian 60 mV per pH at low current densities

evidence.quote: In this current regime, the slopes are equal to the intrinsic Tafel slope of the electrocatalyst material (sET, here assumed being 60 mV per decade), and the potential (vs. NHE) has a Nernstian dependence, i.e., decreases by 60 mV per pH unit.

At constant current density, a decrease in the required electric overpotential by ln(10) e/kT (about 60 mV at room temperature) per pH unit is predicted, as repeatedly observed in experimental studies [29–31].

For very small JBH (JBH << Jmax), X equals cH. Then the proton activity in buffer layer and catalyst (X) corresponds to the pH in the bulk electrolyte so that the local pH is very close to the bulk pH.

props.statement: At very low overpotentials (J << Jmax) the catalytic current is not affected by proton transfer to the bulk electrolyte: the Tafel slope equals the intrinsic Tafel slope, the potential decreases by about 60 mV per pH unit at constant current density, and the local pH stays close to the bulk pH; this Nernstian behaviour has repeatedly been observed experimentally.

props.name: intrinsic Tafel slope: alpha_ET 1.0 ~ 60, 0.5 ~ 120 mV/dec

evidence.quote: For example, an αET value of 1.0 corresponds to about 60 mV per decade (at room temperature); an αET value of 0.5 corresponds to about 120 mV per decade.

props.statement: The intrinsic Tafel slope sET of the catalyst material is set by the electrocatalytic transfer coefficient αET: at room temperature αET = 1.0 corresponds to about 60 mV per decade and αET = 0.5 to about 120 mV per decade.

props.name: Tafel-slope increase at intermediate overpotentials from buffer diffusion

evidence.quote: At intermediate overpotentials, the Tafel slope increases in comparison to its low-overpotential value, which has been assigned before to mass transport limitations and largely can be avoided by the employment of a rotating-disc electrode [28,32–34]. In the described model, the mass transport limitations result from diffusion of protonated and unprotonated buffer bases in the electrolyte, without involving buffer base diffusion within the catalyst ﬁlm.
The use of a rotating disc electrode (or just stirring of the solution) would increase the value of kD.

props.note: the observed increase 'has been assigned before to mass transport limitations' with references [28,32–34] cited by the source
props.statement: At intermediate overpotentials the Tafel slope increases compared with its low-overpotential value; in the model this mass-transport limitation results from diffusion of protonated and unprotonated buffer bases in the electrolyte (not within the catalyst film) and can be reduced by increasing the effective diffusion constant kD, e.g. with a rotating-disc electrode or stirring.

evidence.note: flag basis (attempt-2 fix): with the captions' stated parameters kD = 10 mA cm mol-1 (0.01 A cm mol-1) and B0 = 0.1 M = 0.1 mol L-1 = 1e-4 mol cm-3, Equations (15)-(16) give Jmax = kD B0 KaB/(KaB + cH) < 1e-6 A cm-2 at every pH (about 9.9e-9 A cm-2 at pH 5, 5e-7 at pH 7, 9.9e-7 at pH 9); the curves printed in Figures 2 and 3 instead approach the printed asymptotes 9.9e-6, 9.1e-5, 5e-4 and 9.9e-4 A cm-2 at pH 5, 6, 7 and 9, i.e. kD B0 = 1e-3 A cm-2 scaled by the same unprotonated fraction - a ~1000x internal inconsistency of the source, consistent with B0 = 0.1 M having been evaluated as 0.1 mol cm-3 in the simulation

props.method: numerical evaluation of the model's current–voltage relation (Equation (20)) and of its derivative (Equation (7)) for pH 5.0–9.0 in 0.5 steps; Figure 4 shows the Tafel slope extrapolated to 1 µA cm−2
props.note: Figures 2–4 are simulated curves (calculated per Equation (20) and its derivative), so the digitized result_values have origin 'computed'; produced_by remains the figure-digitization analysis. FLAG (attempt-2 fix): the printed current-density axis of Figures 2 and 3 is internally inconsistent with the captions' stated parameters. Equation (16) with kD = 10 mA cm mol-1 and B0 = 0.1 M = 1e-4 mol cm-3 gives Jmax = kD B0 KaB/(KaB + cH) < 1e-6 A cm-2 at every pH (about 9.9e-9 A cm-2 at pH 5, 5e-7 at pH 7, 9.9e-7 at pH 9), while the printed curves approach the printed asymptotes (9.9e-6, 9.1e-5, 5e-4, 9.9e-4 A cm-2 at pH 5, 6, 7, 9), i.e. kD B0 = 1e-3 A cm-2 scaled by the same unprotonated fraction - consistent with B0 = 0.1 M having been evaluated as 0.1 mol cm-3 in the simulation (~1000x). The digitized values are kept exactly as printed on the figure axes (axis calibration re-verified against the 300-dpi page image of p. 6); they are not rescaled, since values are recorded as printed. Consequently the recorded potentials at J = 1e-5 and 1e-4 A cm-2, the Figure 3 slopes at J >= 1e-6 A cm-2 and the Figure 4 slopes extrapolated at 1 µA cm-2 are unreachable at the stated pH under the captions' literal parameters but are read off the printed curves as such; each affected value carries a note. Attempt-3 verification: the second reading flagged five Figure 3 values and the Figure 4 pH 9 value as inconsistent with Equation (20) and the Figure 2 limiting currents even after the ~1000x B0 correction (p. 6 Figure 3, p. 7 Figure 4). The issue does not hold: Equation (20)'s proton-transport term carries beta^-1 with beta = e/kBT per natural-log unit (Eqs. (3)-(4)), so the decadic Tafel-slope contribution is ln10*beta^-1 = 59.2-60.2 mV dec-1 at 298-303 K (Eq. (6); the paper's own Eqs. (5)/(21) state ~60 mV dec-1 per pH). With the Figure 2 asymptote Jmax values (9.9e-6 and 9.9e-4 A cm-2 at pH 5 and 9), Equation (20) reproduces the printed values: pH 9 slopes 89.5-91.0 (printed 90.8) at J = 1e-5 and 111.7-113.6 (printed 113.3) at J = 5e-5 A cm-2; pH 5 slope 85.1-86.5 (printed 86.0) at J = 3e-6 A cm-2; 120 mV dec-1 crossings at 4.9-5.0e-6 (printed 5e-6, pH 5) and 0.87-1.03e-4 (printed 9e-5, pH 9, within the reading uncertainty and the Jmax asymptote uncertainty) A cm-2; Figure 4 pH 9 at 1 uA cm-2: 64.6-65.7 with Eq. (20) (65.2 with the Eq. (27) approximation) vs printed 65.5. The flagged discrepancy arose from evaluating the proton-transport term with beta^-1 = 25.7 mV dec-1 directly, a factor ln10 too small. Pixel re-measurement of the 300/400-dpi page image (p. 6) confirms each printed curve position (86.3, 91.1, 113.2 mV dec-1; 4.99e-6 and 9.01e-5 A cm-2 at 120 mV dec-1), matching the digitized values.

props.name: buffer-base proton-transport model for near-neutral-pH OER
assumptions: the effective proton concentrations (proton activities) in the catalyst film (region A) and the near-surface buffer layer (region B) are equal at steady state: XCat = XLayer = X
proton transport inside the catalyst film and proton transfer from the film to the solvent are kinetically not limiting (clearly faster than transport over macroscopic distances in the solvent)

protonated and unprotonated buffer are exchanged between the buffer layer and the bulk by diffusion described by one effective diffusion constant kD; all details of the diffusion geometry are covered by kD
the total buffer concentration B0 is the same in all three regions
at steady state the electric current density equals the proton current density (Je = JBH = J)
equations: JBH,L=>S = kD BLH ; JBH,S=>L = kD BSH  (Eqs 11–12)
kD = F D/(del/2), for two parallel electrodes of identical area at distance del  (Eq 14)
JBH = kD B0 [X/(KaB + X) − cH/(KaB + cH)]  (Eq 15)
Jmax = kD B0 [KaB/(KaB + cH)] = kD B0 [BS−/(BS− + BSH)]  (Eqs 16–17)
∆V = sET ln J/Je0 + β−1 ln{[cH + (J/Jmax) KaB]/[1 − (J/Jmax)]}  (Eq 20)
s = d∆V/d ln Je = sET + β−1 d ln X(Je)/d ln Je  (Eq 7)
s = sET + sPT, sPT = β−1 d ln X/d ln J  (Eqs 22–23)
sPT = β−1 J [KDB0 KaB X/(KaB + X)²]⁻¹  (Eq 26); for X = cH: sPT = β−1 J KD/βB  (Eq 27)

evidence.quote: We are aiming at a simple model that describes the inﬂuence of proton transport mediated by buffer molecules on the catalytic activity.

props.model_kind: analytical transport–kinetic model (proton transport by diffusing buffer bases coupled to a Butler–Volmer-type catalytic current)
unmodeled: the idealized two-electrode cell and the spatial concentration profiles of Figure 1 are a schematic illustration (stated illustrative values: maximal BH concentration 100 mM to 1 M, anode–cathode distance about 1 cm, catalyst film about 500 nm, example pH 7); the source gives no numerical concentration profiles
props.validity_domain: OER at near-neutral pH with dissolved buffer bases (stated to apply from about pH 2 to 12, extended to extreme pH by substituting the water species H2O/H3O+ or OH−/H2O as the buffer pair, with increasing imprecision at pH < −1 and pH > 15); proton-transport limitations at the catalyst–electrolyte interface and within the catalyst material are excluded by construction; at high current densities Ohmic electrolyte conductivity is expected to cause further deviations.

props.name: Tafel slope reflects reciprocal buffer capacity; minimum at pKa

evidence.quote: Moreover, the model predicts that at intermediate overpotentials the Tafel slope does not reﬂect the concentration of unprotonated buffer molecules, but rather the pH-buffering capacity of the BH/B−pH-buffer system (Equation (28), Figure 4). This dependence on an effective buffering capacity has not been reported before (to our best knowledge), and it, thus, represents another testable prediction of the presented model.
(4) a Tafel slope that depends on the reciprocal buffer capacity; both predictions are awaiting experimental veriﬁcation.
Equation (27) correctly predicts the minimum of the Tafel slope at pH values close to the pKa of the buffer molecules (Figure 4).

props.note: the source states this dependence 'has not been reported before (to our best knowledge)' and 'still requires experimental verification'
props.statement: At intermediate overpotentials the Tafel slope does not reflect the concentration of unprotonated buffer molecules but the pH-buffering capacity βB of the BH/B− buffer system (Equation (28)); the Tafel slope therefore has a minimum at pH values close to the buffer pKa, and its pH dependence tracks the reciprocal buffer capacity.
